claim: Microglia are brain parenchymal macrophages that originate from the primitive yolk sac.
source: Microglia are brain parenchymal macrophages that are unique among tissue-resident macrophages due to their primitive yolk sack origin, self-renewal properties (Ajami et al., 2007), and independence from adult hematopoiesis (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Schulz et al., 2012; Sheng et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research (Ajami et al., 2007; Ginhoux et al., 2010; Schulz et al., 2012; Sheng et al., 2015).

claim: Microglia have self-renewal properties.
source: Microglia are brain parenchymal macrophages that are unique among tissue-resident macrophages due to their primitive yolk sack origin, self-renewal properties (Ajami et al., 2007), and independence from adult hematopoiesis (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Schulz et al., 2012; Sheng et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ajami et al., 2007.

claim: Microglia are independent from adult hematopoiesis.

claim: Microglial dysfunction is associated with severe brain neuropathologies.

claim: In Alzheimer's disease, microglia form a barrier around amyloid plaques.
source: In neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), microglia form a barrier around amyloid plaques, thereby protecting against the neurotoxicity of aggregated beta-amyloid (Aβ) (Condello et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Condello et al., 2015.

claim: Microglia protect against the neurotoxicity of aggregated beta-amyloid by forming a barrier around amyloid plaques.

claim: Disruption of microglial activity is often related to aging and inflammation.

claim: Disruption of microglial activity leads to increased plaque formation.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deczkowska et al., 2018; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Krasemann et al., 2017.

claim: CD11c+ activated microglia are also known as disease-associated microglia or neurodegenerative microglia.

claim: The appearance of CD11c+ activated microglia correlates with the progression of disease pathology in neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: In Alzheimer's disease, highly phagocytic CD11c+ activated microglia accumulate around Aβ deposits.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kamphuis et al., 2016 and Yin et al., 2017.

claim: CD11c+ activated microglia are highly phagocytic cells.

claim: Accumulation of CD11c+ activated microglia around Aβ deposits mitigates Aβ-associated tau seeding and spreading.

claim: Activated microglia may play a protective role in neurodegeneration.
source: These activated microglia may play a protective role in neurodegeneration, thus implicating targeted manipulation as a therapeutic strategy.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the preceding discussion about the mitigating effects of activated microglia on tau pathology.

claim: Early studies indicated selective migration of monocytic cells toward Aβ plaques.
source: Although the origin of the myeloid cells that accumulate around the Aβ deposits is controversial, early studies indicated selective migration of monocytic cells toward the Aβ plaques (Hohsfield and Humpel, 2015), while more recent research suggests that these cells are derived from resident embryonic-derived microglia (Reed-Geaghan et al., 2020; Shukla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hohsfield and Humpel, 2015.

claim: More recent research suggests that myeloid cells accumulating around Aβ deposits are derived from resident embryonic-derived microglia.
source: Although the origin of the myeloid cells that accumulate around the Aβ deposits is controversial, early studies indicated selective migration of monocytic cells toward the Aβ plaques (Hohsfield and Humpel, 2015), while more recent research suggests that these cells are derived from resident embryonic-derived microglia (Reed-Geaghan et al., 2020; Shukla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Reed-Geaghan et al., 2020 and Shukla et al., 2019.

claim: The origin of myeloid cells that accumulate around Aβ deposits is controversial.

evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by contrasting citations.

claim: Microglia-independent macrophages are found at border regions including the subdural meninges, dura mater, and choroid plexus.
source: In addition to the macrophages in brain parenchyma, microglia-independent macrophages are also found at the border regions, such as the subdural meninges (SDM), including the pia and arachnoid mater, the dura mater (DM), and the choroid plexus (CP) (Brioschi et al., 2020; Utz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brioschi et al., 2020 and Utz et al., 2020.

claim: Border-associated macrophages represent a family of different subpopulations.
source: Single-cell RNAseq analysis revealed that these border-associated macrophages (BAMs) represent a family of different subpopulations (Van Hove et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Van Hove et al., 2019 and mentions single-cell RNAseq analysis.

claim: The contributions of BAMs to CNS integrity and neurodegeneration remain to be elucidated.
source: However, the contributions of BAMs to CNS integrity and neurodegeneration remain to be elucidated.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: APP-KI mice express three human AD-associated mutations that promote progressive accumulation of Aβ.
source: The APP-KI mouse line expresses three human AD-associated mutations that promote the progressive accumulation of Aβ through its increased production of Aβ, particularly the more toxic Aβ42 form, as well as increasing Aβ aggregation and reducing degradation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the mouse model.

claim: APP-KI mice develop progressive Aβ accumulation from 2 months of age.
source: APP-KI mice develop progressive Aβ accumulation from 2 months of age, thus mimicking several aspects of human AD, including microgliosis and synaptic loss (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: APP-KI mice mimic several aspects of human AD, including microgliosis and synaptic loss.
source: APP-KI mice develop progressive Aβ accumulation from 2 months of age, thus mimicking several aspects of human AD, including microgliosis and synaptic loss (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: P2RY12+ microglia are the main CD45int F4/80hi cell population in the brain parenchyma of all mice.
source: P2RY12+ microglia were the main CD45int F4/80hi cell population in the brain parenchyma of all mice and their absolute numbers are significantly enhanced in brains of 12-month-old APP-KI mice due to microgliosis occurring during the development of AD (Sevenich, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the study and citation to Sevenich, 2018.

claim: The absolute numbers of P2RY12+ microglia are significantly enhanced in brains of 12-month-old APP-KI mice.
source: P2RY12+ microglia were the main CD45int F4/80hi cell population in the brain parenchyma of all mice and their absolute numbers are significantly enhanced in brains of 12-month-old APP-KI mice due to microgliosis occurring during the development of AD (Sevenich, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the study and citation to Sevenich, 2018.

claim: Enhanced numbers of P2RY12+ microglia in 12-month-old APP-KI mice are due to microgliosis occurring during the development of AD.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sevenich, 2018 and inference from the data.

claim: AD mice show a substantial increase in the absolute numbers of P2RY12lowCD11c+ activated microglia.
source: AD mice showed also a substantial increase in the absolute numbers of P2RY12lowCD11c+ activated microglia, which were absent in the brain of young mice and constituted only a minor fraction in aged mice (Figure 1A–C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A–C and E.

claim: P2RY12lowCD11c+ activated microglia are absent in the brain of young mice.

claim: CD11c+ activated microglia aggregate around Aβ amyloid plaques.

claim: The appearance of activated microglia during neurodegeneration in APP-KI mice is consistent with reports from other AD transgenic mouse models such as 5xFAD and APP/PS1.
source: In accordance with reports of the appearance of activated microglia during neurodegeneration in other AD transgenic mouse models, such as 5xFAD and APP/PS1 (Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Mrdjen et al., 2018), this phenotype was recapitulated in APP-KI mice in our study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Keren-Shaul et al., 2017 and Mrdjen et al., 2018, and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Enhanced infiltration of BM-derived inflammatory cells in the brain during disease progression was not observed.
source: Surprisingly, we did not observe an enhanced infiltration of BM-derived inflammatory cells in the brain during disease progression.
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in the study.

claim: In aged APP-KI mice, the infiltration by Ly6Chi monocytes and Ly6G+ neutrophils is comparable to that in age-matched controls.
source: Even in aged APP-KI mice, the infiltration by Ly6Chi monocytes and Ly6G+ neutrophils was comparable to that in age-matched controls (Figure 1A–B and E).

claim: A large population of CD206+MHCIIlow BAMs is preferentially localized in the SDM and CP.
source: A large population of CD206+MHCIIlow BAMs was preferentially localized in the SDM and CP, whereas these cells were less abundant in the DM.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Enhanced inflammatory cell infiltration is not caused by aging or neurodegenerative disease progression.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from data shown in Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: YFP signal was barely detectable in the CD45int fraction, which included microglia and activated CD11c+ microglia, in both WT and AD mice.

claim: During AD progression, microglial YFP-labeling remained minimal.

claim: Ongoing neurodegeneration during AD progression does not promote microglial replenishment by BM-derived cells.

claim: Activated CD11c+ microglia maintained a low YFP-labeling profile during AD progression.
source: Similarly, activated CD11c+ microglia, which were increasingly formed during AD progression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C), maintained a low YFP-labeling profile, suggesting that despite their phenotypic shift, these cells preserved their embryonic signature and were not replaced by BM-derived cells during evolution of the disease (Figure 3A–C).

evidence: The claim is based on inference from data showing low YFP-labeling in activated CD11c+ microglia.

claim: Activated CD11c+ microglia are not replaced by BM-derived cells during evolution of AD.

claim: All monocytes are YFP-labeled 2 months after induction, indicating they are exclusively BM-derived.

claim: Fetal-derived MdCs are gradually replaced by BM-derived cells over time and are fully replenished at 8 months post-induction.

claim: There is no significant difference in MdC replenishment between WT and AD mice.

claim: CD11a+ macrophages are BM-derived and show high YFP-labeling.
source: Likewise, CD11a+ macrophages were clearly BM-derived and showed high YFP-labeling and turnover kinetics comparable to monocytes and neutrophils (Figure 3A and B, lower panel, right).

claim: CD11a+ macrophages have turnover kinetics comparable to monocytes and neutrophils.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Activated CD11c+ microglia maintain their embryonic origin in E7.5 embryonic labeling experiments.
source: To verify whether activated CD11c+ microglia retained their fetal lineage, we performed E7.5 embryonic labeling of APP-KI/KitMerCreMer/R26YFP mice and analyzed microglia and activated CD11c+ microglia obtained from disease-affected offspring aged 9 months. Despite the AD-associated pathology, we not only confirmed that activated CD11c+ microglia maintained their embryonic origin, but showed that microglia and activated CD11c+ microglia share the same yolk sac origin, whereas all other tested myeloid cells (monocytes, Mdc, CD11a+ macrophages, and neutrophils) did not arise from embryonic progenitors of the yolk sac (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D from E7.5 embryonic labeling experiments.

claim: Microglia and activated CD11c+ microglia share the same yolk sac origin.
source: To verify whether activated CD11c+ microglia retained their fetal lineage, we performed E7.5 embryonic labeling of APP-KI/KitMerCreMer/R26YFP mice and analyzed microglia and activated CD11c+ microglia obtained from disease-affected offspring aged 9 months. Despite the AD-associated pathology, we not only confirmed that activated CD11c+ microglia maintained their embryonic origin, but showed that microglia and activated CD11c+ microglia share the same yolk sac origin, whereas all other tested myeloid cells (monocytes, Mdc, CD11a+ macrophages, and neutrophils) did not arise from embryonic progenitors of the yolk sac (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D from E7.5 embryonic labeling experiments.

claim: Monocytes, MdCs, CD11a+ macrophages, and neutrophils do not arise from embryonic progenitors of the yolk sac.
source: To verify whether activated CD11c+ microglia retained their fetal lineage, we performed E7.5 embryonic labeling of APP-KI/KitMerCreMer/R26YFP mice and analyzed microglia and activated CD11c+ microglia obtained from disease-affected offspring aged 9 months. Despite the AD-associated pathology, we not only confirmed that activated CD11c+ microglia maintained their embryonic origin, but showed that microglia and activated CD11c+ microglia share the same yolk sac origin, whereas all other tested myeloid cells (monocytes, Mdc, CD11a+ macrophages, and neutrophils) did not arise from embryonic progenitors of the yolk sac (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D from E7.5 embryonic labeling experiments.

claim: Non-parenchymal monocytes, MdCs, and CD11a+ macrophages are swiftly replaced by BM cells, with 100% YFP-positivity at 2 months post-induction.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both CD206+ BAM subpopulations show weaker YFP-labeling compared to other macrophages such as MdCs.
source: In contrast, both CD206+ BAM subpopulations showed weaker YFP-labeling compared to other macrophages such as MdCs, which were already fully replenished within 2 months in all three regions (Figure 4).

claim: In the DM, YFP-labeling is significantly higher in CD206+MHCII+ BAMs than in CD206+MHCIIlow BAMs.

claim: Dural CD206+MHCII+ BAMs are characterized by slow but consistent BM-cell replacement over time, reaching approximately 35% YFP-positivity by 8 months post-induction.

claim: The SDM niche is less accessible to BM-dependent replenishment than the DM.

claim: The DM has a greater capacity to support peripheral cell traffic due to its fenestrated blood vessels.

claim: Skull BM-derived monocytes can contribute to the refilling of dural BAMs.

claim: CP BAM replenishment from BM-derived cells is extremely slow, with YFP signal reaching only 10–15% by 8 months after induction.
